一次 RabbitMQ 投递在 RustStream 服务中的路径：推送、处理器、回复和确认。
RabbitMQ 让消息经由交换机按绑定进入队列，消费者通过连接中的一个信道读取一个队列。
队列向消费者推送投递，每个消费者都有一个未确认投递的窗口，确认会重新打开窗口。
向 RabbitMQ 的一次发布，在帧写出时、服务器确认时或信道事务提交时完成。

direct reply-to 把回复直接发到请求方的信道，不经过回复队列，至多一次。
每种交换机类型读取消息的不同部分来选择队列：路由键、路由键上的模式、什么都不读，或者消息头。
ack、drop、retry 和 retry_after 在 RabbitMQ 上变成什么；在这里，每次结算都是投递所在信道上的一个帧。
The parts of ruststream-lapin a RabbitMQ service uses, one page per component.
With asyncapi the generated document speaks AMQP 0.9.1: the server, the queue behind each channel and the properties of each send.
A subscription's channel is its queue with durability and exclusivity; a publish names a routing key on an exchange, or a queue.
The x-ruststream-amqp extension lists each binding of a subscription: exchange, type, routing key and arguments, in declaration order.
A receive operation reports manual acknowledgement; a send reports the delivery mode, priority and expiration its policy fixes.
The server reports the host and the AMQP version; the credentials and the virtual host of the connection URI stay in the service.
LapinBroker connects a service to RabbitMQ; new only records the URI, and the runtime connects it at startup and shuts it down at the end.
The URI carries credentials, virtual host and scheme; connection_name labels the service in the management UI, over one connection.
declare_topology(true) declares the exchanges, the queue and the bindings a descriptor states; off, the topology is the operator's and must exist.
AmqpError is the crate's one error: connect, publish, subscribe, consume, declare, request, timeout, closed, transaction and options.
One glob, ruststream_lapin::prelude, brings the core prelude, the descriptors, the policies under the family's names and the context keys.
A publisher or requester that outlives the connection reports AmqpError::Closed instead of succeeding against a closed connection.
An amqps URI with one of the tls-native-tls, tls-rustls or tls-rustls-ring features connects over TLS, through lapin's own backends.
Ctx keys give a handler the exchange, routing key, redelivered flag and delivery tag; Context<'_, AmqpContext> reads them all.
bind joins a queue to a RabbitExchange under a routing key; a direct exchange routes on the exact key, and the default exchange on queue names.
bind_with binds a queue to a headers exchange by x-match and the headers to match, all of them or any one.
consistent_hash spreads a stream over queues bound with integer weights, by a hash of the routing key, through the RabbitMQ plugin.
A fanout exchange copies every message to every bound queue and ignores the routing key.
A topic exchange routes on dotted routing-key patterns, where * matches one word and # any number of words.
LapinPublish, Publish in the prelude, sends fire-and-forget: the message name is the routing key, and a publish resolves once the frame is written.
exchange sends a policy's publishes to a named exchange; without it the default exchange delivers to the queue named by the key.
content-type, correlation-id, reply-to and message-id ride their AMQP properties; every other header lands in the header table.
A handler bounds its slot on LapinPublishOptions and adjusts one message's AMQP properties with builder steps over the policy's defaults.
expiration gives one message, or every message of a policy, a TTL after which the broker drops or dead-letters it.
persistent marks a message to survive a broker restart; policies default to persistent, and a request policy to transient.
priority sets the AMQP priority of one message or of every message of a policy; it orders deliveries only on an x-max-priority queue.
LapinRequest, Request in the prelude, gives a handler a requester over direct reply-to that awaits the correlated reply or times out.
DirectReplyTo sends each reply to the address the request named and echoes its correlation id, over a reply type with no destination.
An ack sends basic.ack, a retry basic.reject with requeue, a drop basic.reject without it; RabbitMQ counts every rejection.
dead_letter_exchange gives a queue its own route for every rejected or spent message; dead_letter_routing_key overrides the key.
delay(Delay::dlx_ttl()) parks a delayed copy in a broker waiting queue under a TTL, which dead-letters it back when it fires.
A quorum queue ends a poison loop itself: delivery_limit, or max_attempts with dead_letter, becomes its x-delivery-limit.
Delay::plugin_dme waits in the delayed-message-exchange plugin instead, so a short delay never queues behind a long one.
On a classic queue max_attempts and dead_letter are the runtime's: it counts the copies it publishes back to the queue by name.
retry_after redelivers no sooner than a delay; with no delay on the queue the service holds the copy, at most once over the window.
A queue name in #[subscriber] consumes that existing queue as a classic queue; a descriptor carries every other setting.
argument and arguments pass any x- declaration argument the descriptor does not model, such as a TTL or a length limit, verbatim.
A slice handler gets a batch assembled on the client, up to the mount site's size or until batch_wait (50 ms) passes since the first delivery.
workers(n, by_key) keeps deliveries that share the amqp-partition-key header on one lane, in order, while other keys run in parallel.
prefetch caps unacknowledged deliveries per subscription on the broker or one descriptor; unset, the server applies no limit.
RabbitQueue consumes a classic queue: its durability, exclusivity, auto-delete, bindings and the settings shared with quorum queues.
RabbitQuorumQueue consumes a replicated quorum queue, which is always durable and counts the deliveries each message spends.
TestApp::start runs the production app on LapinBroker in process, with exchanges, bindings, requeues, quorum counts and reply-to.
TestApp::start_live runs the same test body against a running RabbitMQ, one subscription per queue, for what only a server has.
A handler bounded Out<impl TransactionalPublisher> begins a scope, publishes and commits; the mount site picks confirms or a server transaction.
ConfirmsPublish, TransactionalPublish in the prelude, resolves each publish once the broker confirmed it and commits by awaiting every confirm.
owned_transaction opens independent confirm transactions on one publisher; each settles on its own, and commit consumes it.
ServerTxPublish uses AMQP channel transactions: publishes become visible together at commit, paid for with a synchronous round trip.

ruststream-lapin 如何测量自己：三个循环、在真实节点上的运行、受 Broker 限制的算式，以及代码的计数。这套流程属于整个框架（RustStream 的方法论），本页说明它在 RabbitMQ 上是什么样子。

同一个进程把每个场景跑三遍，三个循环只有一处不同：由什么来传递消息。 裸客户端。 手写的循环直接驱动 lapin：消费、解码、ack。 Broker crate。 本 crate，上面什么都没有：Broker 建立连接，队列描述符打开订阅，一个循环从订阅的流里取出投递，解码并 ack。 RustStream。 用户写的服务：一个 #[subscriber] 处理器和包住它的应用。 其余一切在三个循环里都相同：连接、订阅分到的信道、队列参数、预取窗口、ack 的位置、解码成同一个类型、载荷字节、tokio 运行时和二进制文件。 消息体是 512 字节的 JSON，发布时不要求持久化。经典队列把它放在内存里；仲裁队列除了自己的复制存储，没有别的模式。

每次运行一个新队列。 每次运行都声明自己的队列，跑完就删掉，所以没有哪个循环会去处理上一次运行留下的东西。 测量窗口从第一次投递开始，到最后一条投递上的工作完成时结束，三个循环都是如此。每个循环都在这一刻之后才确认投递，所以在一次运行的数百万次确认中，有一次在每个循环里都落在数字之外。 消息条数由一次探测决定，使每一次被测量的运行在任何机器上都至少持续五秒。 三个循环交错进行：裸客户端、crate、RustStream，共三轮。每个循环报告自己的最佳、中位和最差一轮。 当裸客户端把这次运行花在等待服务器、而不是干活上时，这一行标为 受 Broker 限制。这是一道算式：在各轮之外做一次探测，测出服务器应答一个 basic.qos 要多久；当一次投递所需的往返加起来不少于一条消息所花时间的一半时，就打上这个标记。往返时间与机器信息一起公布，所以这道算式可以核对。AMQP 投递不需要等待自己的往返，因为服务器主动推送消息体，也不应答确认。它要等的是确认换回来的额度，而预取窗口把这份等待摊到窗口里的每一条消息上。

开销图的每个场景都是用户写的服务，跑在连接到 compose 环境中节点的 LapinBroker 上，构建时不带 testing feature。服务在启动时声明一个经典队列，用对照中相同的预取窗口消费它，并运行在单线程的 tokio 运行时上。在服务处理任何消息之前，另一个线程先把队列填满，填充要等节点确认了每一条消息才结束。 指令数来自 callgrind，内存分配次数来自 DHAT。一个场景先跑一次投递，再跑 1000 次，再跑 2000 次。后两次之差是一条消息的稳态开销，单次投递就是冷启动。 真实的节点按自己的节奏应答，所以服务线程等待套接字的频率每次运行都不一样。同一份代码运行七次，一次运行的指令数最多变动 2.4%，内存分配最多变动一个块。每个场景的分配下限比它测到过的最大值高出千分之一，分配次数超过这个下限时，just bench-code 失败。加上 --baseline=main 时，指令数多出百分之五以上，recipe 也会失败；不带基线的运行不限制指令数。失败的运行照样打印表格，并在表格下面列出它超出的每一项限制，旧值与新值并排。

同一行的三个循环可以互相比较，因为它们在同一个进程里、在同一个节点上交错运行。一行不能与另一个 Broker crate 公布的一行比较：不同的传输在每条消息上做的工作不同。 标为 无法区分 的开销，是该循环与裸客户端之间的差值小于两者各自多次运行之间的波动。低于运行间噪声的数字会让人误以为有一种从未测到过的精度，所以不公布。 标为 受 Broker 限制 的一行，是裸客户端在大部分运行时间里都在等待服务器。这时 crate 和运行时的工作发生在这段等待之中，差值接近零。这是开销的下限，而不是对它的测量。
指令数包括本 crate 的代码、它上面的运行时，以及 lapin 在服务线程上做的工作。这些数字是绝对值，框架自身的开销也算在内；框架单独的开销由核心库在它的基准测试页面上公布。同样的指令数在缓存未命中时要花更多时间，所以指令数不等于时间。 每个数字都是稳态值，即 1000 次投递的运行与 2000 次投递的运行之差。建立连接、打开信道、声明队列和注册消费者属于冷启动，只付出一次。

一行只是一个队列上的一个消费者、一个很小的消息体，以及一个跑在回环地址上的节点。它测的是一次投递在本 crate 中的开销，而不是 RabbitMQ 能承载多少。 预取窗口决定了这些绝对数值。如果消费者确认每一条消息，并且同一时刻只允许持有一条未结算的投递，那么每条消息都要花掉一次往返，三个循环都会落在这次往返的速度上。这些运行使用的宽窗口，才让传输之上的开销得以显现；改动窗口，每一列都会一起变化。 这些数字是一台机器在某一天的快照，构建信息记录在旁边。它们由人工在一台专门用于这次运行的机器上重新测量：它们显示的差值，比共用机器上的噪声还小。

每个订阅打开自己的信道，并在上面启动一个消费者。在消费者启动之前，订阅用 basic.qos 发送它的窗口：RabbitQueue::prefetch 用于单个队列，LapinBroker::prefetch 用于所有没有自行设置的订阅。这个设置是一个非零数，所以两者都没有设置的订阅不发送 basic.qos，以不限制的方式运行。 窗口也限制批的大小。AMQP 没有批帧，所以批处理器的一批在客户端上，从队列已经推送过来的投递中组装：最多到挂载点指定的大小，或者在 batch_wait（默认 50 毫秒）内到达的数量。窗口小于批大小时，批的上限就是窗口。 订阅被释放时关闭它的信道，RabbitMQ 把它持有而未结算的投递重新入队。运行时如何结算每次投递，见结算与重试。 协议规则来自 RabbitMQ（消费者预取、消费者确认、工作队列）。
启用连接恢复后，Lapin 恢复消费者现有的信道、已声明的交换机、队列和绑定，并在恢复投递前重新应用预取设置。 消费者流等待可恢复的断连，重试耗尽时以消费错误结束。恢复关闭时，遵循普通 Lapin 消费者的终止行为。 断连后仍然存在的队列中的未确认投递可能再次投递。旧的确认在重连后可能失败；处理器必须容忍重复处理。 发布不会自动重发，等待中的 RPC 请求的截止时间继续计算。

发布策略决定模式，更强的模式就是另一个策略： 策略 信道 发布何时返回 LapinPublish 连接上所有这类发布者共用的一个信道 帧写出之后 ConfirmsPublish 自己的信道，处于确认模式 服务器确认之后；否定确认是一个错误 ServerTxPublish 自己的信道，处于事务模式 在事务内，提交时 发布者确认或事务信道在第一次发布时打开，所以从不发布的策略不持有信道。每次发布都不带 mandatory，所以已确认的发布仍可能没有到达任何队列：确认表示服务器收下了消息，而不是有队列持有它。除非策略另行指定，消息都是持久化的。 信道错误会关闭信道，连接保持不变。一次发往不存在的交换机的发后即忘发布就足以触发它，而发布者看不到服务器的应答。下一次发布会打开一个新信道。带着未完成的事务而失效的事务信道是个例外：事务存在于这个信道上，所以提交会失败，而不是报告成功。 ConfirmsPublish 的事务是服务中的一个缓冲区。提交按顺序发布缓冲的消息，并等待每一个确认。它对每条消息是持久的，但不是原子的：在失败的那条之前发出的消息仍然是已发布的。ServerTxPublish 的事务是 RabbitMQ 自己的事务。每个信道只有一个，因为 tx.select 让信道本身进入事务模式。 协议规则来自 RabbitMQ（发布者确认、事务）。

经典队列位于一个节点上，什么都不统计；仲裁队列是复制的，会统计失败的投递，并自行移走用尽次数的消息。 并排对比经典队列与仲裁队列：各自在哪里保存消息，重新入队做了什么，以及什么会结束一条反复回来的消息超过上限经典队列仲裁队列一个节点保存消息带 requeue 的 reject：回到队列，不计数不带 requeue 的reject：转为死信或丢弃一个主节点及其从节点，基于 Raft带 requeue 的 reject：回到队列，x-delivery-count + 1超过投递上限：转为死信或丢弃从 RabbitMQ 4.0 起，仲裁队列的投递上限默认为 20，除非队列另行设置 以文字阅读本图 经典队列: 一个节点 保存消息; 带 requeue 的 reject： 回到队列， 不计数; 不带 requeue 的 reject：转为 死信或丢弃 仲裁队列: 一个主节点及其 从节点，基于 Raft; 带 requeue 的 reject： 回到队列， x-delivery-count + 1; 超过投递 上限：转为 死信或丢弃 带 requeue 的 reject： 回到队列， x-delivery-count + 1 → 超过投递 上限：转为 死信或丢弃: 超过上限 从 RabbitMQ 4.0 起，仲裁队列的投递上限 默认为 20，除非队列另行设置 队列的类型在声明时通过 x-queue-type 参数确定。两种类型接受同样的消费者和同样的结算帧。它们的区别在于消息保存在哪里，以及重新入队让消息付出什么代价。 在 RabbitMQ 4 中，经典队列把消息保存在一个节点上，不做复制。带 requeue 被拒绝的投递会回到队列，并且可以无休止地反复回来。队列不保存计数：重新投递只带有 redelivered 标志。 仲裁队列用 Raft 协议把消息复制到多个节点，每次写入都要得到其中法定数量节点的接受。它天然是持久的。它统计每条消息失败的投递次数，并在重新投递时把计数写进 x-delivery-count 消息头。计数超过队列投递上限的消息会离开队列。从 RabbitMQ 4.0 起，队列没有设置上限时，上限为 20。 从 RabbitMQ 4.3 起，并不是每次退回都计数。basic.reject，以及在投递未结算时关闭的信道，都会计数。带 requeue 的 basic.nack 退回消息但不计数。 因不带 requeue 的拒绝或超过投递上限而离开队列的消息，在队列有死信交换机时进入该交换机（x-dead-letter-exchange，可选配 x-dead-letter-routing-key）。没有死信交换机的队列会丢弃它。

队列类型是一个描述符类型，因为它决定了重试做什么：RabbitQueue 对应经典队列，RabbitQuorumQueue 对应仲裁队列。仲裁队列的描述符没有 durable、exclusive 和 auto_delete 步骤，因为仲裁队列总是持久的、共享的。 本 crate 用 basic.reject 结算否定的结果，从不使用 basic.nack。对单次投递，这两个帧做的事相同，而在仲裁队列上只有拒绝才计数。因此处理器的 retry() 会用掉消息的一次投递，队列的上限会结束一条一直失败的消息。结算与重试用图说明了每种类型如何响应重试。 队列的规则来自 RabbitMQ（经典队列、仲裁队列、毒消息处理、死信交换机）。

The parts of ruststream-lapin a RabbitMQ service uses, one page per component: the broker (LapinBroker), its queue descriptors, its publish policies and the in-process transport a TestApp test runs on.

With the asyncapi feature the generated document speaks AMQP 0.9.1: the server, the queue behind each channel and the properties of each send. The core builds the AsyncAPI document from the app, before anything connects. This crate adds the specification's amqp binding, version 0.3.0, to the parts it knows about. The server reports the host and the AMQP version. A channel reports the queue behind a subscription, or the exchange a publish leaves through. An operation reports how a receive settles and which properties a send carries. The exchanges a queue is bound to ride the crate's own extension, x-ruststream-amqp. Everything comes from the service's own declarations: the broker, the queue descriptors and the publish policies. The document is published and shared, so no binding carries a credential. The binary #[ruststream::app] writes prints the document with asyncapi gen.

The dependency line: ruststream-lapin = { version = "0.7", features = ["asyncapi"] } The service registers its broker under the label rabbit, the key of its server in the document. cargo run --example lapin_asyncapi --features asyncapi -- asyncapi gen prints the document. A subscription's channel is its queue with durability and exclusivity; a publish names a routing key on an exchange, or a queue. A subscription's channel binding is is: queue. Its queue object carries the name and the durable, exclusive and autoDelete settings of the RabbitQueue descriptor. A channel the service publishes to is described from its publish policy. Its name is the destination the mount site resolved: a reply's name, the name of a slot entry, or a dead_letter(..) declaration. On a policy with a named exchange, the name is the routing key: the binding is is: routingKey with the exchange's name. On the default exchange the routing key is the queue a message lands in: the binding is is: queue with that queue's name. A queue's settings belong to the side that declares it, so this binding carries the name alone. A reply under DirectReplyTo goes to the address each request carries. Its channel therefore has no address, and the receive operation names the header the address is read from.

The channel inventory.check reports a transient, exclusive, auto-delete queue. The reply channel inventory.unrouted reports the exchange answers, and the dead-letter channel inventory.dead reports the queue of that name. The x-ruststream-amqp extension lists each binding of a subscription: exchange, type, routing key and arguments, in declaration order. The specification's channel binding is a queue or a routing key, and it has no field for what joins the two. So a subscription reports its bindings in this crate's extension, beside the amqp binding of its channel. The extension holds a bindings list with one entry per bind and bind_with, in the order the descriptor declares them. An entry carries the exchange name and its type: direct, fanout, headers, topic, or the type a plugin exchange declares. The routingKey is written even when it is empty, because an empty key is the binding key of a fanout or a headers exchange. The arguments appear when the binding has any, each value in the JSON shape of its AMQP type. A subscription with no binding has no extension. An extension is not a binding, so it carries no bindingVersion.

The queue inventory.events is bound to a topic exchange by its key and to a headers exchange by its arguments. A receive operation reports manual acknowledgement; a send reports the delivery mode, priority and expiration its policy fixes. Every receive operation carries ack: true. This crate acknowledges each delivery by hand, so the handler's outcome settles it. A slot entry and a dead-letter destination each have a send operation. Its binding carries the properties every message through the policy takes. deliveryMode is 2, persistent, unless the policy sets persistent(false), which gives 1. priority and expiration, in milliseconds, appear when the policy fixes a priority or an expiration. The document describes the declaration, so a step that adjusts one message leaves it as it is. A reply is the reply of its receive operation. Under DirectReplyTo the reply's address has the location $message.header#/reply-to: a client reads the address from the request's reply-to header.

The operation receive_inventory_check reports ack: true and a reply addressed by reply-to. The operation send_inventory_events_inventory_restock reports delivery mode 2, priority 4 and an expiration of 30000. Macros Manual examples/lapin_asyncapi.rs fn service(broker: LapinBroker) -> RustStream { let inventory = AppInfo::new("inventory", "1.0.0"); RustStream::new(inventory).with_broker_labeled("rabbit", broker, |b| { b.include(check) .max_attempts(nonzero!(3u32)) .dead_letter("inventory.dead") .out_reply(Publish::default().exchange("answers")) .transform(DirectReplyTo); b.include(on_event) .out( Restocks, Publish::default() .priority(4) .expiration(Duration::from_secs(30)), ) .build(); }) } examples/manual/lapin_asyncapi.rs fn service(broker: LapinBroker) -> RustStream { let inventory = AppInfo::new("inventory", "1.0.0"); RustStream::new(inventory).with_broker_labeled("rabbit", broker, |b| { let check = subscriber(checks(), Check).reply().to("inventory.unrouted"); b.include(check.build()) .max_attempts(nonzero!(3u32)) .dead_letter("inventory.dead") .out_reply(Publish::default().exchange("answers")) .transform(DirectReplyTo); b.include(subscriber(events(), OnEvent).build()) .out( Restocks, Publish::default() .priority(4) .expiration(Duration::from_secs(30)), ) .build(); }) }

The server reports the host and the AMQP version; the credentials and the virtual host of the connection URI stay in the service. A broker registered with with_broker_labeled is a server of the document, under its label. Its host is the host and port of the connection URI. The user, the password, the virtual host and the query of the URI stay out of it. A URI with no port gives the host alone. The protocol is amqp, and protocolVersion is 0.9.1. AMQP 1.0 is a different protocol with a binding of its own, so the version tells a reader which one a client speaks here.

The broker connects as the user inventory to the virtual host prod. Its server in the document is rabbit:5672, protocol amqp, version 0.9.1. LapinBroker connects a service to RabbitMQ; new only records the URI, and the runtime connects it at startup and shuts it down at the end. LapinBroker::new takes the connection URI. It does no I/O, so the whole service fits the synchronous #[ruststream::app] builder. The settings that follow it are builder steps too: a connection name, a default prefetch window and declare_topology. At startup the runtime connects the broker and receives a ConnectedLapinBroker. The connect opens the AMQP connection and logs in, so an unreachable server or a refused login fails startup instead of the first delivery. Every subscription and every publisher of the service opens against that connected form. At shutdown the runtime closes the connection and receives a ClosedLapinBroker. #[subscriber("orders")] consumes the queue orders. The queue has to exist on the server, unless the broker declares the topology. The descriptors that bind a queue to an exchange or choose its type are on the Subscriptions pages.

The service consumes the queue orders on a server at localhost:5672. cargo run --example lapin_broker_service --features testing -- run starts it. Macros Manual examples/lapin_broker_service.rs use ruststream_lapin::prelude::*; #[subscriber("orders")] async fn place(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "order placed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672"), |b| { b.include(place); }, ) } examples/manual/lapin_broker_service.rs use ruststream_lapin::prelude::*; struct Place; impl Handle<Order> for Place { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order placed"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672"), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Place).build()); }, ) }

The URI carries the credentials, the virtual host and the scheme; connection_name labels the service in the management UI. The URI has the form amqp://user:password@host:port/vhost. A URI without credentials logs in as guest, and RabbitMQ admits guest only from localhost. A URI without a virtual host connects to the default one, /. The amqps scheme opens the connection over TLS. A URI that does not parse fails startup with AmqpError::Connect, in a test as on a server. connection_name is the name the management UI lists for the connection. A connection without one is listed by its client address and port. One connection carries the whole service. Each subscription opens a channel of its own on it. Fire-and-forget publishes share one channel. A confirms or server-transaction publisher opens its own channel on first use, because both modes are channel state.

Recovery is off by default. Enable it with auto_recover(true). Lapin restores the connection, channels, declared exchanges, queues, bindings, prefetch, publisher confirms and consumers. Existing handles stay usable; the application and its startup hooks do not restart. Retries use Lapin's exponential backoff. The default limit is 16 retries, configurable with recovery_retries(n). The limit applies to the initial connection and later reconnects. Zero allows an attempt without retrying; a successful connection resets the retry budget. With recovery off, the initial connection is attempted once. Exhausting startup retries returns AmqpError::Connect; exhausting recovery ends the affected consumer stream with AmqpError::Consume. Set a heartbeat in the URI, such as ?heartbeat=30, so RabbitMQ and Lapin can detect silent connection loss. ConnectedLapinBroker::is_connected() is a synchronous connection check for readiness: it is false while disconnected or after shutdown. A true result does not guarantee that channel and topology restoration has finished, or that workers are healthy. Lapin can restore a publisher channel before another channel has recreated an exclusive queue and its binding. A publish in that window can be confirmed but unroutable: RabbitMQ discards it, so it is neither queued nor redelivered. Publisher confirms alone do not prove that a route exists. Keep production topology provisioned independently of the reconnecting connection, or establish that the route is ready before sending application messages. This cross-channel recovery ordering is tracked in Lapin issue #481. A failed publish is not replayed, outstanding RPC deadlines keep running, and server transactions require recovery to remain disabled.

The service logs in as orders on the virtual host shop, enables recovery with 32 retries, and requests a 30-second heartbeat. Macros Manual examples/lapin_broker_connection.rs /// The user `orders` on the virtual host `shop`; the management UI lists the connection as /// `orders-svc`. fn broker() -> LapinBroker { LapinBroker::new("amqp://orders:secret@localhost:5672/shop?heartbeat=30") .connection_name("orders-svc") .auto_recover(true) .recovery_retries(32) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker(), |b| { b.include(place); }) } examples/manual/lapin_broker_connection.rs /// The user `orders` on the virtual host `shop`; the management UI lists the connection as /// `orders-svc`. fn broker() -> LapinBroker { LapinBroker::new("amqp://orders:secret@localhost:5672/shop?heartbeat=30") .connection_name("orders-svc") .auto_recover(true) .recovery_retries(32) } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Place).build()); }) }

declare_topology(true) declares the exchanges, the queue and the bindings a descriptor states; off, the topology is the operator's and must exist. The setting is off by default. A descriptor then states the topology the service expects, and the service creates nothing. A subscription to a queue the server does not have fails startup with AmqpError::Subscribe. With the setting on, each subscription declares its topology before it starts consuming. It declares the exchanges its bindings name, then the queue, then the bindings, in that order. The built-in amq.* exchanges and the default exchange are never declared: the server already has them. A declaration repeats safely while the descriptor matches what the server holds. A queue or an exchange declared again with other settings is refused by the server with PRECONDITION_FAILED, and startup fails with AmqpError::Declare. RabbitMQ 4 refuses a transient queue that is not exclusive, so a RabbitQueue declared durable(false) has to be exclusive(true) too. Some settings exist only as declaration arguments, so they reach the server only from a service that declares. A quorum queue's delivery limit and the waiting queue of a delayed redelivery are two of them. The in-process transport finds every queue a subscription names, so a test shows no missing queue. A declaration the server refuses is refused in process too.

The service declares the topic exchange events, the queue orders and the binding order.* between them. Macros Manual examples/lapin_broker_declare_topology.rs use ruststream_lapin::prelude::*; #[subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("orders").bind(RabbitExchange::topic("events"), "order.*"))] async fn place(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "order placed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { // The service owns `events`, `orders` and the binding between them. let broker = LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672").declare_topology(true); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(place); }) } examples/manual/lapin_broker_declare_topology.rs use ruststream_lapin::prelude::*; struct Place; impl Handle<Order> for Place { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order placed"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { // The service owns `events`, `orders` and the binding between them. let broker = LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672").declare_topology(true); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { let orders = RabbitQueue::new("orders").bind(RabbitExchange::topic("events"), "order.*"); b.include(subscriber(orders, Place).build()); }) }

AmqpError is the crate's one error: connect, publish, subscribe, consume, declare, request, timeout, closed, transaction and options. Each variant names the step that failed. The lapin error behind it is its source, so the client library's types stay out of the crate's API. Variant When Connect the URI did not parse, the server was unreachable or refused the login, or the close failed Publish the server refused a message, such as a body over its 16 MiB max_message_size, or did not confirm it Subscribe a channel, its prefetch or its consumer could not be opened, such as on a queue the server does not have Consume an open consumer failed to receive Declare the server refused an exchange, a queue or a binding the service declares Request a request could not be sent, or its reply could not be received RequestTimeout no reply arrived within the requester's deadline Closed a publisher or a requester was used after the shutdown; it names the target Transaction a transaction call came out of order: a commit with none open, or a second begin InvalidOptions the settings cannot work together, such as half of a quorum queue's retry declaration A service meets the error in two places. A failed startup carries it as the source of the runtime's error, and the service exits before it consumes anything. A publish from a handler returns it inside the core's PublishError, and the handler decides how the delivery settles. The enum is #[non_exhaustive], so a match on it ends with a wildcard arm. With automatic recovery enabled, transient disconnects pause consumers. When retries run out, a consumer stream yields a terminal AmqpError::Consume and ends. Pairing ServerTxPublish with auto_recover(true) fails with AmqpError::InvalidOptions; direct server-transaction operations reject that combination too.

A shipment the server refuses is logged with its cause, and the order is dropped to the queue's dead-letter exchange. Macros Manual examples/lapin_broker_errors.rs #[subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("orders").dead_letter_exchange("orders.failed"))] async fn ship(order: &Order, Out(shipments): Out<impl Publisher, Shipments>) -> HandlerOutcome { let shipment = Shipment { order_id: order.id, labels: (1..=order.parcels) .map(|parcel| format!("{}-{parcel:07}", order.id)) .collect(), }; if let Err(err) = shipments.message(&shipment).publish().await { // The error names the step that failed and the server's reason. tracing::warn!(subscription = "orders", order.id, error = %err, "shipment not published"); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/lapin_broker_errors.rs struct Ship; impl<Entry> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(Entry,)>> for Ship where Entry: OutEntry<Shipments, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let shipment = Shipment { order_id: order.id, labels: (1..=order.parcels) .map(|parcel| format!("{}-{parcel:07}", order.id)) .collect(), }; if let Err(err) = outs.get(Shipments).message(&shipment).publish().await { // The error names the step that failed and the server's reason. tracing::warn!(subscription = "orders", order.id, error = %err, "shipment not published"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); } Ok(()) } } fn orders() -> RabbitQueue { RabbitQueue::new("orders").dead_letter_exchange("orders.failed") }

One glob, ruststream_lapin::prelude, brings the core prelude, the descriptors, the policies under the family's names and the context keys. use ruststream_lapin::prelude::*; is the one import a RabbitMQ routes file writes. It carries the core's own prelude, so #[subscriber], RustStream, HandlerOutcome and Out come with it. It adds LapinBroker, the descriptors RabbitQueue and RabbitQuorumQueue, RabbitExchange, Delay and DirectReplyTo. It adds the context keys Exchange, RoutingKey, Redelivered and DeliveryTag, and the argument types AMQPValue and FieldTable. It also carries the transaction traits a handler settles a transaction with. The publish policies come under the names every broker crate uses: Publish is LapinPublish, TransactionalPublish is ConfirmsPublish, and Request is LapinRequest. So a mount site reads the same on every broker. ServerTxPublish keeps its own name: an AMQP server transaction is a guarantee of its own, not a second spelling of TransactionalPublish. Two broker preludes in one file collide on the uniform names; the prefixed types at the crate root tell them apart. A handler body bounds its slots with capability traits, such as Out<impl TransactionalPublisher>, and names no broker type. The one exception is a body that sets an AMQP property for a single message: it bounds its slot Out<impl Publisher<Options = LapinPublishOptions>, Marker> and calls the steps of LapinPublishSteps, both from this prelude.

The routes file reads the routing key through a context key and replies through TransactionalPublish, all from the one glob. Macros Manual examples/lapin_broker_prelude.rs use ruststream_lapin::prelude::*; #[subscriber( RabbitQueue::new("orders").bind(RabbitExchange::topic("events"), "order.*"), reply )] async fn confirm(order: &Order, Ctx(routing_key): Ctx<RoutingKey>) -> Confirmation { tracing::info!(order.id, %routing_key, "order confirmed"); Confirmation { id: order.id } } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672"), |b| { b.include(confirm) .out_reply(TransactionalPublish::default()); }, ) } examples/manual/lapin_broker_prelude.rs use ruststream_lapin::prelude::*; struct Confirm; impl Handle<Order, Confirmation, (), AmqpContext> for Confirm { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, AmqpContext>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Confirmation, HandlerOutcome>> { let routing_key = ctx.context(RoutingKey); tracing::info!(order.id, %routing_key, "order confirmed"); ready(Ok(Confirmation { id: order.id })) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672"), |b| { let orders = RabbitQueue::new("orders").bind(RabbitExchange::topic("events"), "order.*"); b.include(subscriber(orders, Confirm).reply().build()) .out_reply(TransactionalPublish::default()); }, ) }

A publisher or requester that outlives the connection reports AmqpError::Closed instead of succeeding against a closed connection. At shutdown the runtime stops the subscriptions and lets the handlers in flight finish. Then it closes the connection with the AMQP close handshake. A delivery the service received and never settled goes back to its queue when its channel closes, so another consumer gets it. A publisher handed out before the shutdown can outlive it: a task the service spawned keeps it, or a clone of a requester does. Every use of such a handle after the shutdown returns AmqpError::Closed, which names the routing key, the queue or the exchange the call targeted. The connection is marked closed before the handshake starts, so no message slips into a connection that is going away. A tool that drives the broker by hand receives a ClosedLapinBroker from the shutdown; its handshake tells an orderly close from a connection the server had already dropped. If shutdown starts during a reconnect, it marks the broker closed and wakes waiting consumers without waiting for RabbitMQ to return. Existing publishers and requesters then return AmqpError::Closed. If Lapin reconnects afterward, the connection is closed in the background; if retries run out, cleanup ends. No AMQP close handshake is reported for a connection that was unavailable at shutdown.

A heartbeat task takes its publisher at startup and runs past the service's shutdown; its first publish after the shutdown fails with AmqpError::Closed, and the task ends. Macros Manual examples/lapin_broker_shutdown.rs /// Announces the service every 30 seconds until a publish fails; after shutdown that failure is /// `AmqpError::Closed`. async fn heartbeat(publisher: LapinPublisher) { let mut ticks = interval(Duration::from_secs(30)); loop { ticks.tick().await; let beat = Heartbeat { service: "orders".to_owned(), }; if let Err(err) = publisher.message(&beat).publish().await { tracing::info!(error = %err, "heartbeat stopped"); return; } } } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672"), |b| { b.include(place); // The task keeps its publisher past the service's shutdown. b.after_startup(Publish::default(), async move |publisher| { tokio::spawn(heartbeat(publisher)); Ok::<_, Infallible>(()) }); }, ) } examples/manual/lapin_broker_shutdown.rs /// Announces the service every 30 seconds until a publish fails; after shutdown that failure is /// `AmqpError::Closed`. async fn heartbeat(publisher: LapinPublisher) { let mut ticks = interval(Duration::from_secs(30)); loop { ticks.tick().await; let beat = Heartbeat { service: "orders".to_owned(), }; if let Err(err) = publisher.message(&beat).publish().await { tracing::info!(error = %err, "heartbeat stopped"); return; } } } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672"), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Place).build()); // The task keeps its publisher past the service's shutdown. b.after_startup(Publish::default(), async move |publisher| { tokio::spawn(heartbeat(publisher)); Ok::<_, Infallible>(()) }); }, ) }

An amqps URI with one of the tls-native-tls, tls-rustls or tls-rustls-ring features connects over TLS, through lapin's own backends. Each feature turns on one TLS backend of the lapin client: Feature Backend tls-native-tls the platform's TLS library: OpenSSL on Linux, Secure Transport on macOS, SChannel on Windows tls-rustls rustls with the aws-lc-rs crypto provider, checking the server against the platform's trusted roots tls-rustls-ring rustls with the ring crypto provider A service enables one of them on its ruststream-lapin dependency, for example features = ["tls-rustls"]. RabbitMQ listens for TLS on port 5671 by default, so an amqps URI usually names that port. The URI keeps the form of a plain connection: credentials, host, port and virtual host. The handshake happens when the runtime connects the broker at startup. A certificate the client does not trust fails startup with AmqpError::Connect. The in-process transport opens no socket: it parses the amqps URI as the real connect does and runs the service's handlers without a handshake.

The service connects to rabbit.example.com over TLS, as the user orders on the virtual host shop. Macros Manual examples/lapin_broker_tls.rs /// The `amqps` scheme on the server's TLS port, 5671: the connection opens with a TLS /// handshake. fn broker() -> LapinBroker { LapinBroker::new("amqps://orders:secret@rabbit.example.com:5671/shop") } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker(), |b| { b.include(place); }) } examples/manual/lapin_broker_tls.rs /// The `amqps` scheme on the server's TLS port, 5671: the connection opens with a TLS /// handshake. fn broker() -> LapinBroker { LapinBroker::new("amqps://orders:secret@rabbit.example.com:5671/shop") } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Place).build()); }) }

Ctx keys give a handler the exchange, routing key, redelivered flag and delivery tag; Context<'_, AmqpContext> reads them all. AmqpContext carries what a delivery has beside its payload and its headers. The subscription builds it once per delivery. A handler binds one field with Ctx<K>, where K is a key of context::keys: Key Value What it is Exchange String the exchange the message was published to, empty for the default exchange RoutingKey String the routing key the message was published with Redelivered bool whether the server handed the message out before DeliveryTag u64 the delivery's number on its channel The four keys are in the prelude. A body that reads several fields takes ctx: &mut Context<'_, AmqpContext> instead and calls ctx.context(key) per field, as the manual form does; there the exchange and the routing key are borrowed &str. AmqpContext itself comes from ruststream_lapin::context. The routing key tells apart the messages a topic binding takes. Redelivered is set on a delivery a classic queue hands out again after a retry; a quorum queue counts deliveries instead. The delivery tag numbers the deliveries of one channel, so it identifies a delivery only within its subscription.

The handler replies with where each order came from. Macros Manual examples/lapin_context.rs use ruststream_lapin::prelude::*; /// Records where each order came from: its exchange and routing key, and whether the server had /// handed it out before. #[subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("orders"), reply)] async fn audit( order: &Order, Ctx(exchange): Ctx<Exchange>, Ctx(routing_key): Ctx<RoutingKey>, Ctx(redelivered): Ctx<Redelivered>, Ctx(delivery_tag): Ctx<DeliveryTag>, ) -> AuditRecord { tracing::info!(order.id, %exchange, %routing_key, redelivered, delivery_tag, "order audited"); AuditRecord { order_id: order.id, exchange, routing_key, redelivered, } } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672"), |b| { b.include(audit).out_reply(Publish::default()); }, ) } examples/manual/lapin_context.rs use ruststream_lapin::prelude::*; /// Records where each order came from: its exchange and routing key, and whether the server had /// handed it out before. struct Audit; impl Handle<Order, AuditRecord, (), AmqpContext> for Audit { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, AmqpContext>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<AuditRecord, HandlerOutcome>> { let exchange = ctx.context(Exchange); let routing_key = ctx.context(RoutingKey); let redelivered = ctx.context(Redelivered); let delivery_tag = ctx.context(DeliveryTag); tracing::info!(order.id, %exchange, %routing_key, redelivered, delivery_tag, "order audited"); ready(Ok(AuditRecord { order_id: order.id, exchange: exchange.to_owned(), routing_key: routing_key.to_owned(), redelivered, })) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672"), |b| { let orders = RabbitQueue::new("orders"); b.include(subscriber(orders, Audit).reply().build()) .out_reply(Publish::default()); }, ) }

bind joins a queue to a RabbitExchange under a routing key; a direct exchange routes on the exact key, and the default exchange on queue names. A publisher sends a message to an exchange, never to a queue. The exchange copies the message into the queues bound to it whose bindings match. RabbitExchange names the exchange of a binding, and its constructor names its type: Constructor Routes on direct the exact routing key topic a dotted pattern of the routing key fanout nothing: every bound queue gets every message headers the message's headers, against the binding's arguments consistent_hash a hash of the routing key, through a plugin bind(exchange, routing_key) adds a binding to a queue descriptor, and a queue may carry several. A direct exchange delivers a message to every queue bound under its routing key exactly; a message under a key no queue is bound under goes nowhere. The default exchange, with the empty name, is a direct exchange every queue is bound to under its own name. So a message published with no exchange reaches the queue its routing key names, and a binding to the default exchange is refused. An exchange is durable by default and survives a broker restart, and auto_delete is off. The exchange and its bindings reach the server when the broker declares the topology; the built-in amq.* exchanges are bound to and never declared. The publishing side names its exchange on the publish policy with exchange, and the message's name is its routing key. RabbitExchange::custom(name, kind) names an exchange of a type a server plugin provides, such as x-random or x-modulus-hash. A queue binds to it with bind, or with bind_with for a plugin that routes on binding arguments. The plugin does the routing, so the server needs the plugin enabled, and the in-process transport routes nothing through such an exchange.

bind_with binds a queue to a headers exchange by x-match and the headers to match, all of them or any one. A headers exchange ignores the routing key and routes on the message's headers. bind_with(exchange, routing_key, arguments) gives the binding an argument table, a FieldTable of AMQPValue entries. The entry x-match decides the rule: all takes a message that carries every other entry of the table with the same value, and any takes a message that carries at least one. The other entries are the headers to match, and the routing key of the binding is usually empty. A plain bind to a headers exchange sends an empty table, and all of no headers is true of every message, so such a queue gets everything the exchange gets. The publishing side sets the headers on the message, and they ride the AMQP header table the exchange reads. bind_with also serves a plugin exchange that routes on binding arguments.

The EU gold queue matches both headers, and the EU-or-gold queue matches either one. consistent_hash spreads a stream over queues bound with integer weights, by a hash of the routing key, through the RabbitMQ plugin. The constructor exists with the crate's plugin-consistent-hash feature and names the x-consistent-hash type of the rabbitmq_consistent_hash_exchange plugin. The server needs the plugin enabled: rabbitmq-plugins enable rabbitmq_consistent_hash_exchange. Each queue binds with its weight as the routing key, such as "1" or "2", and takes that share of the hash space. The exchange hashes the routing key of each message, so messages with one key always reach the same queue. So a key such as a customer or an account keeps its messages in one queue, in order, while the stream spreads over all of them. Within one service instance, lanes give the same per-key order without the plugin. The plugin does the routing on the server. The in-process transport declares the exchange and its bindings and routes nothing through it, so a test of the spread runs against a plugin-enabled server with TestApp::start_live.

Orders are hashed by customer over two shards of equal weight. A fanout exchange copies every message to every bound queue and ignores the routing key. A queue binds to a fanout exchange with any routing key, usually the empty one. Each bound queue gets its own copy, and each copy is consumed and settled on its own. So a fanout exchange is the broadcast of RabbitMQ: one event, many independent consumers. A service that needs a copy in every instance binds an exclusive queue per instance.

A price change reaches both the search index and the cache, each through a queue of its own. A topic exchange routes on dotted routing-key patterns, where * matches one word and # any number of words. A routing key of a topic exchange is a list of words separated by dots, such as order.created or order.shipped.late. A queue binds with a pattern of the same shape. * stands for exactly one word, and # for zero or more words. So order.* takes order.created and passes order.shipped.late by, and order.# takes both. A pattern without wildcards matches its key exactly, as on a direct exchange. A message that matches several bindings of one queue reaches that queue once. A handler that serves several keys reads the key of each delivery through the RoutingKey context key.

Order steps go to the topic exchange events as order.<step>; the audit queue takes every one-word step, and the shipping queue takes order.shipped alone. LapinPublish, Publish in the prelude, is the fire-and-forget publish policy: a publish resolves once the frame is written, with no broker confirm. The message name is the routing key, and the exchange belongs to the policy. By default that is the default exchange, where a routing key addresses the queue of the same name; exchange names another. The policy holds no connection. At startup the runtime pairs it with the connected broker into a LapinPublisher, which publishes on the connection's shared publish channel. A publisher kept past shutdown answers every publish with AmqpError::Closed. A mount site names the policy wherever a registration publishes: .out_reply(Publish::default()) for a reply, .out(Slot, Publish::default()) for a slot, .out_retry(Publish::default()) for retry copies. It is also the broker's default policy, so a registration that names none replies and retries through it. Where a reply goes is a property of the reply type, as the core's replies page describes. A publish outside a handler goes through after_startup on the broker scope: once the subscriptions are open, the runtime pairs the policy and hands the hook the live publisher. The policy holds the defaults of the per-message properties. confirms and server_tx move to the transactional policies and keep these settings. Automatic recovery restores publisher channels and confirms, but does not replay failed publishes. A publish during an outage can return an error, and the outcome of an in-flight publish can be uncertain. An application that retries must account for possible duplicates. Connection readiness alone does not mean every publisher channel has finished recovering. A recovered publisher channel can also precede binding restoration on another channel; a confirmed publish can then be unroutable and discarded, as described under connection recovery.

Every order is answered with a confirmation, routed under the name the reply type declares. Once its subscriptions are open, the service announces itself. Macros Manual examples/lapin_publishing_publish.rs /// Every order is answered with a confirmation, routed under the name its type declares. #[subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("orders"), reply)] async fn confirm(order: &Order) -> Confirmation { tracing::info!(order.id, "order confirmed"); Confirmation { order_id: order.id } } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672"), |b| { b.include(confirm).out_reply(Publish::default()); // Once the subscriptions are open, the service announces itself. b.after_startup(Publish::default(), async move |publisher| { let started = Started { service: "orders".into(), }; publisher.message(&started).publish().await }); }, ) } examples/manual/lapin_publishing_publish.rs /// Every order is answered with a confirmation, routed under the name its type declares. struct Confirm; impl Handle<Order, Confirmation> for Confirm { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Confirmation, HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order confirmed"); ready(Ok(Confirmation { order_id: order.id })) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672"), |b| { let confirm = subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("orders"), Confirm); b.include(confirm.reply().build()) .out_reply(Publish::default()); // Once the subscriptions are open, the service announces itself. b.after_startup(Publish::default(), async move |publisher| { let started = Started { service: "orders".into(), }; publisher.message(&started).publish().await }); }, ) }

exchange sends a policy's publishes to a named exchange instead of the default exchange. The message name stays the routing key, and the exchange routes by it. A topic exchange matches it against binding patterns, a direct exchange matches it exactly, and a fanout exchange ignores it. Without exchange, the default exchange delivers to the queue whose name equals the routing key. RabbitMQ accepts a publish that matches no binding and drops it. Every publish policy of the crate takes the setting: ConfirmsPublish, ServerTxPublish and LapinRequest too. With declare_topology(true), the subscription that binds a queue to the exchange declares the exchange.

Every accepted order is announced on the events topic exchange under order.placed. An audit queue bound under order.* receives it. if events.message(&placed).publish().await.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// The audit service's queue takes every `order.*` event from that exchange. #[subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("orders.audit").bind(RabbitExchange::topic("events"), "order.*"))] async fn audit(placed: &OrderPlaced) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(placed.id, "order placed"); b.include(audit); }) } examples/manual/lapin_publishing_exchange.rs /// Every accepted order is announced on the `events` exchange under `order.placed`. struct Accept; impl<Egress> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(Egress,)>> for Accept where Egress: OutEntry<DefaultSlot, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(Egress,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let placed = OrderPlaced { id: order.id }; let events = outs.get(DefaultSlot); if events.message(&placed).publish().await.is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } Ok(()) } } /// The audit service's queue takes every `order.*` event from that exchange. struct Audit; impl Handle<OrderPlaced> for Audit { fn handle( &self, placed: &OrderPlaced, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(placed.id, "order placed"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { let broker = LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672").declare_topology(true); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { let audit = RabbitQueue::new("orders.audit").bind(RabbitExchange::topic("events"), "order.*"); b.include(subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("orders"), Accept).build()) .out(DefaultSlot, Publish::default().exchange("events")) .build(); b.include(subscriber(audit, Audit).build()); }) }

A publish's headers travel in the AMQP frame: content-type, correlation-id, reply-to and message-id ride the native properties of those names, and every other header lands in the header table. A handler hands the headers to the publish builder with .with_headers(..), as a HeaderMap or as the typed contract its message declares. The four identity headers become properties, so a consumer written against another client finds them where the protocol puts them. Every other header is a byte string in the header table, so a binary value survives the round trip. A delivery reports both kinds back as headers, and the handler reads them from its context. A delivery also reports two properties under headers of their own: the priority under PRIORITY_HEADER (amqp-priority) and the TTL under EXPIRATION_HEADER (amqp-expiration). A header never sets a delivery property: priority, expiration and delivery mode are properties of the policy and the publish builder. An AMQP property is a short string of at most 255 bytes, and a longer identity header fails the publish with AmqpError::InvalidOptions before anything is routed.

The invoice carries the order's reference as its message-id property and the tenant in the header table. The billing side reads both from its context. Macros Manual examples/lapin_publishing_headers.rs /// The invoice carries the order's reference as its `message-id` property and the tenant in the /// header table. #[subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("orders"))] async fn issue_invoice(order: &Order, Out(invoices): Out<impl Publisher>) -> HandlerOutcome { let mut headers = HeaderMap::new(); headers.insert("message-id", order.reference.clone()); headers.insert("tenant", "acme"); let invoice = Invoice { order_id: order.id }; if let Err(err) = invoices .message(&invoice) .with_headers(headers) .publish() .await { // A reference longer than a short string is refused, and a retry will not shorten it. tracing::error!(order.id, %err, "invoice refused"); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// The billing side reads both where it reads every header. #[subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("invoices"))] async fn bill(invoice: &Invoice, ctx: &mut Context<'_>) -> HandlerOutcome { let reference = ctx.headers().get_str("message-id").unwrap_or_default(); let tenant = ctx.headers().get_str("tenant").unwrap_or_default(); tracing::info!(invoice.order_id, reference, tenant, "invoice billed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")).with_broker( LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672"), |b| { b.include(issue_invoice) .out(DefaultSlot, Publish::default()) .build(); b.include(bill); }, ) } examples/manual/lapin_publishing_headers.rs /// The invoice carries the order's reference as its `message-id` property and the tenant in the /// header table. struct IssueInvoice; impl<Egress> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(Egress,)>> for IssueInvoice where Egress: OutEntry<DefaultSlot, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(Egress,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let mut headers = HeaderMap::new(); headers.insert("message-id", order.reference.clone()); headers.insert("tenant", "acme"); let invoice = Invoice { order_id: order.id }; let invoices = outs.get(DefaultSlot); if let Err(err) = invoices .message(&invoice) .with_headers(headers) .publish() .await { // A reference longer than a short string is refused, and a retry will not shorten it. tracing::error!(order.id, %err, "invoice refused"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); } Ok(()) } } /// The billing side reads both where it reads every header. struct Bill; impl Handle<Invoice> for Bill { fn handle( &self, invoice: &Invoice, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { let reference = ctx.headers().get_str("message-id").unwrap_or_default(); let tenant = ctx.headers().get_str("tenant").unwrap_or_default(); tracing::info!(invoice.order_id, reference, tenant, "invoice billed"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")).with_broker( LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672"), |b| { b.include(subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("orders"), IssueInvoice).build()) .out(DefaultSlot, Publish::default()) .build(); b.include(subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("invoices"), Bill).build()); }, ) }

LapinPublishSteps adds priority, expiration and persistent to the publish builder, so a handler sets an AMQP property of one message. A publish policy holds the defaults for every message it sends, and a step adjusts one message over them. LapinPublishOptions holds the three settings, each optional: what a call leaves alone keeps the policy's value. The steps exist on a publisher whose options type is LapinPublishOptions. So the handler bounds its slot Out<impl Publisher<Options = LapinPublishOptions>, Slot> and still names no publisher type. The steps come from this crate's prelude, the one prelude a handler body imports besides the framework's. The values reach the frame as protocol fields, never as headers. The publish still leaves through the slot's own entry, with its codec and transforms. A test reads the options back with with_options on tb.out::<Slot>().

An expedited order leaves at priority 9 and expires after an hour. An ordinary order takes the policy's priority 3. expiration gives one message a time to live; LapinPublish::expiration gives one to every message of a policy. A message nobody consumed within its TTL leaves the queue. The broker drops it, or dead-letters it where the queue has a dead-letter exchange. RabbitMQ expires a message when it reaches the head of its queue. A policy that sets no TTL sends messages that do not expire. AMQP counts the TTL in whole milliseconds, and a shorter non-zero TTL becomes one millisecond. A delivery reports it under EXPIRATION_HEADER in milliseconds.

persistent sets the delivery mode of one message; LapinPublish::persistent sets it for every message of a policy. A persistent message (delivery mode 2) on a durable queue survives a broker restart. A transient message (delivery mode 1) does not. The publish policies default to persistent. LapinRequest defaults to transient: a request nobody waits for after its timeout gains nothing from a restart.

priority sets the AMQP priority of one message; LapinPublish::priority sets it for every message of a policy. A policy that sets no priority sends none. RabbitMQ orders deliveries by priority only on a queue declared with x-max-priority, and a higher priority counts as that maximum. On any other queue the priority travels to the consumer and orders nothing. A delivery reports it under PRIORITY_HEADER as decimal digits, and the handler reads it like any other header. A delayed redelivery keeps the priority its original delivery reported.

LapinRequest, Request in the prelude, gives a handler a requester: it publishes a request over RabbitMQ direct reply-to and awaits the correlated reply. The handler bounds its slot Out<impl RequestReply> and calls request with a message and a timeout. At startup the runtime pairs the policy into a LapinRequester. Each request goes out with reply-to set to the amq.rabbitmq.reply-to pseudo-queue and a generated correlation-id. The reply that carries that id resolves the call, and a reply with an id nobody waits for is dropped. No reply within the timeout fails the call with AmqpError::RequestTimeout. One task per requester reads the replies, started by its first request on the runtime the broker connected on. The request carries bytes, so the example encodes the question and decodes the answer with the core's JSON codec. The policy takes exchange, priority and expiration like a publish policy. Requests are transient by default, and persistent(true) makes them persistent. Direct reply-to is at-most-once: the reply state lives on the requester's channel on one node, and nothing is queued durably. A channel that drops loses the replies in flight, and the caller sees a timeout. The responder is any service that answers at the received reply-to with the same correlation-id, as DirectReplyTo does.

DirectReplyTo is a reply transform: it sends each reply to the address the request named in reply-to and echoes the request's correlation-id. It mounts on the reply position: .out_reply(policy).transform(DirectReplyTo). The handler is an ordinary reply handler and knows nothing about the requester. The transform names the destination of every reply, so it mounts only over a reply type that declares none. Over a type with its own #[outgoing(name = "..")] the mount does not compile. The name in the mount site's reply("..") is the fallback: a request without reply-to is answered there, and the generated AsyncAPI document reports it. A LapinRequest requester and a requester on another stack both name the reply address this way. With automatic recovery, the reply dispatcher resumes after Lapin restores its channel and direct reply-to consumer. Deadlines of requests already waiting for replies keep running during the outage; recovery does not restart them or replay their requests. A reply lost during a disconnect may therefore end in AmqpError::RequestTimeout.

The inventory service answers every stock check at the address the request named. A request without one is answered at inventory.check.unrouted. A handler's answer settles its AMQP delivery with a protocol frame: ack sends basic.ack, retry sends basic.reject with requeue, and drop sends basic.reject without it. The frame goes out on the channel the delivery arrived on, and the service publishes nothing. A requeued message goes back to its queue, which hands it out again with the redelivered flag set. The next delivery may reach this consumer or another consumer of the same queue. A handler reads the flag through the Redelivered key of the delivery context. A dropped message leaves the queue: RabbitMQ discards it, or routes it to the queue's dead-letter exchange. The crate settles with basic.reject and never with basic.nack. On one delivery the two frames do the same thing, but RabbitMQ counts a rejected delivery as spent and does not count a nacked one. So a handler that keeps asking for its message back runs down a quorum queue's delivery limit. A quorum queue stamps a returned message with the x-delivery-count header; a classic queue keeps no count, only the flag. A retry under a cap and a delayed retry travel as copies instead of a requeue. After a connection loss, a delivery's old acknowledgement belongs to the old channel and can fail even if the connection has recovered. RabbitMQ requeues unsettled messages from queues that survive the disconnect and may deliver them again. Do not treat reconnection as proof that the old delivery was settled; handlers must tolerate redelivery when recovery is enabled.

An order is requeued the first time it arrives and acknowledged when it comes back redelivered. An order without a SKU is dropped. Macros Manual examples/lapin_settlement_outcomes.rs /// An order without a SKU is rejected for good. Any other order is requeued once, the first time /// it arrives, and acknowledged when the queue hands it out again marked redelivered. #[subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("orders"))] async fn reserve(order: &Order, Ctx(redelivered): Ctx<Redelivered>) -> HandlerOutcome { if order.sku.is_empty() { tracing::warn!(order.id, "order without a SKU, rejected"); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } if !redelivered { tracing::info!(order.id, "stock not counted yet, back to the queue"); return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } tracing::info!(order.id, "reserved"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("stock", "0.1.0")).with_broker( LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672"), |b| { b.include(reserve); }, ) } examples/manual/lapin_settlement_outcomes.rs /// An order without a SKU is rejected for good. Any other order is requeued once, the first time /// it arrives, and acknowledged when the queue hands it out again marked redelivered. struct Reserve; impl Handle<Order, (), (), AmqpContext> for Reserve { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, AmqpContext>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { let outcome = if order.sku.is_empty() { tracing::warn!(order.id, "order without a SKU, rejected"); Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()) } else if !ctx.context(Redelivered) { tracing::info!(order.id, "stock not counted yet, back to the queue"); Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()) } else { tracing::info!(order.id, "reserved"); Ok(()) }; ready(outcome) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("stock", "0.1.0")).with_broker( LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672"), |b| { b.include(subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("orders"), Reserve).build()); }, ) }

dead_letter_exchange gives a queue its own route for the messages it rejects: the x-dead-letter-exchange argument. A drop settles with basic.reject without requeue, and the queue publishes the message to that exchange. The route belongs to the queue, so it takes every message the queue dead-letters, whatever the cause. Besides a rejection, RabbitMQ dead-letters a message whose TTL expired, one pushed out by a length limit, and one that spent a quorum queue's delivery limit. The message keeps its routing key, unless dead_letter_routing_key names another (x-dead-letter-routing-key). The dead-letter exchange routes like any other exchange: a queue bound to it under that key collects the messages. RabbitQuorumQueue takes the same two settings. Both settings are queue arguments. The queue gets them when the service declares it, with declare_topology(true) on the broker. A queue the operator provisions carries the arguments it was declared with. The dead_letter(name) step of the mount chain is a different thing: the destination of a registration's retry cap.
